skills.name: Measure the speed of sound and use echoes

note.text:
An echo is a sound reflected from a large surface such as a cliff or a wall.
Echo method: stand a measured distance d from a wall, clap, and time the echo. The sound travels to the wall and back, a distance of 2d, in time t, so v = 2d/t.
Gun-firing method: an observer a measured distance d away starts a stopwatch when the flash is seen and stops it when the bang is heard. Light arrives almost instantly, so v = d/t.
Echo sounding (sonar) finds the depth of the sea: a pulse is sent down and the time for its return is measured, so depth = vt/2. It is also used to find shoals of fish and, as ultrasound, to look inside the body.
In air, sound travels at about 340 m/s; it goes faster in warmer air.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to measure the speed of sound by the echo and gun-firing methods, and use echoes to find a distance or a depth.
Builds on: Lesson {13} (how sound travels) and Form Three speed, distance and time.
Leads to: ultrasound scanning and sonar, and the wave calculations of Form Five.

sections.heading: Two ways to measure the speed
sections.text:
Echo method: measure the distance d from a large wall or cliff. Clap, and time the gap until the echo returns. The sound travels to the wall and back, a distance of {2}d, so
v = {2}d ÷ t.
Clapping in a steady rhythm so that each clap falls with the echo, and timing many claps, makes the result more reliable.
Gun-firing method: an observer stands a measured distance away, starts a stopwatch on seeing the flash and stops it on hearing the bang. Light travels so fast that its own travel time can be ignored, so
v = d ÷ t.
Both give about {340} m/s in air, and sound travels a little faster in warmer air.

sections.heading: Using echoes
sections.text:
If the speed is known, the same idea gives a distance:
• A shout returns from a cliff after {2} s, with v = {340} m/s. The sound covered {680} m there and back, so the cliff is {340} m away.
• Echo sounding on a ship: a pulse is sent to the sea bed and the echo timed. depth = v × t ÷ {2}. At {1500} m/s, an echo after {0.4} s means a depth of {300} m.
The same method finds shoals of fish, and as ultrasound it is used to look inside the body.
Always remember to halve: the sound covers the distance twice.

key_words.meaning: a sound reflected back from a surface
finding a depth or distance by timing a reflected pulse
sound above about {20000} Hz, too high to hear

examples: {170} m from a wall, echo after {1} s: v = {340} m/s
echo after {0.5} s at {1500} m/s: depth {375} m

mistake.wrong: echo {2} s after a clap {340} m away gives v = {340} ÷ {2} = {170} m/s
mistake.why: The sound travels to the wall and back, so the distance is {2}d.

worked_example.problem: A pupil claps {d} m from a cliff and hears the echo {t} s later. Find the speed of sound in air.
steps: The sound travels to the cliff and back, so the distance is {2} × {d} = {2 * d} m.

cards.idea: An echo is a reflected sound; the sound covers twice the distance to the surface.
example: a clap {170} m from a cliff returns after {1} s: v = {340} ÷ {1} = {340} m/s

cards.idea: Echo method: v = {2}d ÷ t. Gun method: v = d ÷ t, because the flash arrives almost at once.
example: flash seen, bang heard {2} s later, {680} m away: v = {340} m/s
a pulse at {1500} m/s returning after {0.4} s: depth {300} m

check.prompt: A ship sends a sound pulse to the sea bed and receives the echo {t} s later. Sound travels at {v} m/s in sea water. Find the depth, in metres.

misconceptions.explain: That is the whole path down and back; the depth is half.

solution: The pulse travels down and back, so the total path is {v} × {t} = {v * t} m.
The depth is half of that: {answer} m.

questions.prompt: A pupil claps {d} m from a wall and hears the echo after {t} s. Find the speed of sound, in m/s.

misconceptions.explain: The sound covers the distance TWICE: there and back.

solution: The sound goes to the wall and back: {2} × {d} = {2 * d} m.

questions.prompt: A gun is fired {d} m away. The flash is seen, and the bang is heard {t} s later. Find the speed of sound, in m/s.

misconceptions.explain: There is no echo here: the sound travels one way only.

solution: Light reaches the observer almost at once, so the time measured is the time for the sound.
The sound travels {d} m one way.

questions.prompt: A clap is heard as an echo {t} s after it is made. Taking the speed of sound as {v} m/s, how far away is the reflecting wall, in metres?

misconceptions.explain: {v * t} m is the whole path there and back: halve it.
The path is twice the distance to the wall, so halve it once only.

solution: In {t} s the sound covers {v} × {t} = {v * t} m.
That is to the wall and back, so the wall is half as far.

questions.prompt: A ship sends a sound pulse to the sea bed and receives the echo {t} s later. Sound travels at {v} m/s in sea water. Find the depth, in metres.

misconceptions.explain: That is the whole path down and back; the depth is half.

solution: The pulse travels down and back, so the total path is {v} × {t} = {v * t} m.
The depth is half of that: {answer} m.

questions.prompt: A man stands {d} m from a cliff. Taking the speed of sound as {v} m/s, how long after his shout does he hear the echo, in seconds?

misconceptions.explain: The echo has to come back as well: use {2}d.

solution: The sound travels to the cliff and back: {2} × {d} = {2 * d} m.
